Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette: Mateo was sixty when the silver sedan crossed the center line and struck his van on the driver's side. He had been driving back from a zoning meeting in downtown Oakland, his Oceania heritage anchoring him to the multilingual community networks he organized, when the impact threw him forward. The airbags burst, and the world narrowed to the groan of twisting metal and the sharp sting of glass. He remembers the driver's door buckling inward with crystalline precision, the way the steering wheel bit into his ribs, but the ten minutes after the crash simply dissolve into white static. Emergency responders arrived quickly, their navy blue and khaki uniforms bright against the asphalt, and while they worked to extricate him, Mateo kept watching their epaulets and service badges, certain that the shape of their uniforms dictated whether he would live or not. He had been the one who opened the door too early, the one who pushed past the paramedic's steady hand, and the guilt settled heavily in his chest. He was certain the event happened because of the way he acted, not merely the other driver's speed or the wet road. In the months that followed, Mateo's body began keeping time with the accident. It kept reacting as if he were still trapped in the van, his pulse jumping at sudden noises, his shoulders stiffening whenever a conversation turned heated. He noticed it first in his neighborhood, where community meetings grew increasingly common. He organized gatherings for local residents, navigating grant applications, tenant disputes, and city council briefings, but he found himself stepping back from the room when voices rose. Even calm expressions of anger made his breath catch; a neighbor's measured frustration over a broken streetlamp felt just as threatening as a shout. He avoided the community center's main hall when uniformed police officers conducted patrols nearby; the sight of their pressed jackets and service badges consistently pulled the old tension back into his limbs. His memories of the crash refused to settle into a neat story. Some fragments returned with sharp clarity-the screech of tires, the flash of a reflective vest-while longer stretches remained completely blank, no matter how hard he tried to reach them. When asked to describe what had happened, he would pause, his jaw working, certain he knew the sequence but unable to find the words to hold it together. By the time he turned sixty-three, the accumulation of these experiences had hollowed him out. He moved through his days with a quiet detachment, feeling dead inside the way he had read about in clinical charts, as though a layer of glass separated him from the world. His divorce had been finalized two years prior, and though the legal paperwork was settled, the distance remained. He continued his work as a community organizer, coordinating block cleanups and tenant assemblies, but the occupational demands had quietly reshaped his routine. He stopped attending the evening planning sessions where city officials and local police reviewed development proposals, preferring to review maps and schedules alone at his desk. The consequences were practical and visible: his colleagues covered his notes, and he stopped leading the Saturday street fairs where crowds gathered near the traffic wardens. With a PCL-5 scoring forty-nine, his clinical profile aligned closely with his lived reality, yet he did not look to the numbers for answers. He finally sat down in a therapist's office, not because his body was failing, but because he was tired of bracing for a second impact. He hopes to find a way to let his daily life settle, to trust that the present moment is separate from the wrecked van, but his greatest fear remains the sudden flare of anger-either his own or someone else's-that might prove, once again, that he was never truly out of danger.
